report:
## Conclusion

The claim that ibuprofen worsens COVID-19 infection is **not supported by evidence** and is considered false/misleading by major health authorities.

The concern originated in March 2020 when French Health Minister Olivier Véran warned against NSAIDs, citing a speculative hypothesis (published as a letter in *The Lancet*) that anti-inflammatories might upregulate ACE2 receptors, the entry point SARS-CoV-2 uses to infect cells (gh.bmj.com/content/5/6/e002564). This triggered global alarm, but it was based on theoretical biology, not clinical data.

Subsequently, the World Health Organization, FDA, EMA, and Health Canada all reviewed the evidence and found no proven link between ibuprofen and worsened COVID-19 outcomes. WHO stated it does "not currently believe there is any proven scientific evidence linking over-the-counter use of ibuprofen to the aggravation of COVID-19," and the FDA said it was "not aware of scientific evidence" supporting the claim (https://www.sciencealert.com/who-recommends-to-avoid-taking-ibuprofen-for-covid-19-symptoms; https://www.cbc.ca/news/health/ibuprofen-covid-19-novel-coronavirus-1.5501496).

Later, larger observational studies confirmed this. A CIDRAP-reported study found ibuprofen and other NSAIDs were not associated with worse COVID-19 severity or death, though also found no clear benefit, concluding that prior cautionary advice should be reconsidered (https://www.cidrap.umn.edu/ibuprofen-other-nsaids-not-tied-worse-covid-illness-death). Some outlets (e.g., Full Fact, NHS guidance at the time) noted lingering caution due to incomplete direct evidence, favoring paracetamol as a precaution rather than because ibuprofen was proven harmful.

**Bottom line:** Current scientific consensus holds that ibuprofen does not worsen COVID-19; the original warning was precautionary and hypothesis-driven, not evidence-based.
